In this validation execution, active exceeds static by 15.43 percentage points and wrist-only by 18.36 points. Initial camera positioning exceeds continued active control by 8.79 points. These are observed differences for one trained seed; they do not establish a general ranking.

Sensing conditionWhat the policy receives / controls
Wrist onlyWrist RGB and proprioception, with recurrent memory.
Static + wristWrist RGB plus a fixed external view (view 7). The fixed view is a diagnostic candidate; a trained best-static search was not completed.
Active + wristWrist RGB plus the camera-arm image; policy commands the camera throughout the episode.
Initial positioning + wristPolicy selects camera position during the first 1 s, then camera targets freeze. External images, wrist images, proprioception and GRU continue updating. This is not a single-snapshot condition.

All share a 1 s inspection pause and nominal 3.5 s horizon at 25 Hz, 128×96 policy images, and four hidden prong offsets (XM/XP/YM/YP, ±15 mm along the indicated axis). The actor has no privileged offset/goal state. Physical success requires body-position error within 2 mm at three consecutive control samples. This checks sampled holding, not continuous dwell between samples.

Active and initial policies often approach XM closely yet miss the strict hold requirement. The latest static repair’s passive diagnostic similarly finds 7/128 XM episodes sample below 2 mm at least once, but none sustain three samples; median closest sampled XM error is 2.248 mm. This distinguishes near-goal approach from valid insertion.

A privileged scripted controller in actual Warp succeeds on 503/512 (98.24%) matched first episodes: XM 119/128, all other variants 128/128. Its nine failures are XM approaches in a high-goal-X corner, with roughly 63 mm body error and 53–55 mm derived TCP tracking error. This establishes sampled control feasibility, including most XM worlds; it does not identify why the learned policies fail. GPU feasibility audit.

Hyperparameter search: every completed stage

LR/entropy tuning improved measured validation performance over its matched baseline, but no configuration solved all variants. At 751 updates, corrected physical scores are 25.20% / 21.29% for fixed LR and 23.44% / 25.78% for higher entropy, versus 3.91% / 5.08% baseline. Their ordering reverses across numerical repeats; neither is a robust winner.

All four cases use static view 7 + wrist, training seed 0, N512, GRU, clean plug insertion. Initial action std is 0.4, with 4 PPO epochs and 8 minibatches. The fixed-LR case changes both the initial LR and its schedule; it does not isolate schedule alone. The first screen uses 100 updates / 1,228,800 transitions. Each longer run has 751 total updates / 9,228,288 transitions, including the initial 100 (651 additional updates / 7,999,488 transitions).

Learning curves and training quality

Original conditionReward: first 100 updatesReward: last 100 updatesDescriptive plateauMeasured training GPU-hours
Wrist only0.6681.572Yes2.18
Static + wrist (view 7)0.5113.644Yes2.33
Active + wrist0.6645.477Yes2.64
Initial positioning + wrist0.6606.503Yes2.70

All four original reward curves rose and passed the recorded descriptive tail-300 plateau heuristic. Their low physical validation success shows that a reward plateau is not a competence criterion. All spend the last 100 updates at the adaptive LR floor; narrow action distributions motivate exploration diagnostics without proving a failure cause.

Latest repair reward rises from 0.3167 to 6.4986 across the first/last 100-update windows. The final 100 updates contain 4,900 successes / 15,362 completed training episodes (31.90%). Its tail-300 fitted reward change (1.0245) exceeds the plateau tolerance (0.6174), so the recorded plateau heuristic fails. That does not authorize a budget extension.

Corrected objective training curves

The plateau rule requires both fitted tail-300 change and final-150 versus prior-150 mean change to be within 10% of max(0.1, absolute tail reward mean). It is descriptive, not a statistical convergence test. Original histories · Objective repair histories · Fresh repair history.

Camera and memory interventions

These evaluations keep the original trained model_1499 weights frozen. Each row has two independent numerical executions of the same validation initial states; all use physical scoring.

Frozen-checkpoint interventionRepeat 1Repeat 2XM
Active: nominal18.75% (96/512)19.92% (102/512)0/128 in both
Active: freeze targets at 1 s3.32% (17/512)3.52% (18/512)0/128 in both
Initial: nominal29.69% (152/512)29.10% (149/512)0/128 in both
Initial: stale external after 1 s29.69% (152/512)28.91% (148/512)0/128 in both
Initial: reset whole GRU every step1.17% (6/512)1.95% (10/512)0/128 in both

Freezing the active policy’s camera targets after 1 s reduces success by 15.43 / 16.41 percentage points. It also changes camera embodiment/contact and allows joints to settle, so this is not a pure visual causal effect. Holding the initial policy’s external image after 1 s changes success by 0 / −0.20 points; wrist sensing, proprioception and GRU remain live. Resetting its whole GRU every step drops success by 28.52 / 27.15 points, but also changes inspection and view selection.

These checks show dependence of specific checkpoints on camera commands or memory. They do not establish that continuous active control beats retrained initial-only or feedforward alternatives. All intervention metrics · Intervention audit.

Historical scores, limitations and provenance

Why older success rates differ

Original model_1499Historical derived-substep scoreSeparate corrected physical execution
Wrist only0.59% (3/512)1.56% (8/512)
Static + wrist (view 7)11.52% (59/512)4.49% (23/512)
Active + wrist27.54% (141/512)19.92% (102/512)
Initial positioning + wrist36.13% (185/512)28.71% (147/512)

An audit found that the historical derived-state rule could flag success while current physical qpos lay outside 2 mm. The physical rule fixes sampling, but re-evaluation also changes trajectories numerically. Historical scores remain archived and are not pooled with current-qpos scores. Every physical success reported in this digest has zero recorded distance, hold, three-sample and raw-qpos violations.

All SO-101 scientific comparisons here use one training seed, exploratory validation, and clean occlusion. Repeated execution can change episode outcomes despite identical initial states and images. Wilson intervals describe episode-count uncertainty within an execution; they do not capture training-seed, simulator or selection uncertainty. A searched static baseline, independent training seeds and untouched test evaluation remain missing.

Legacy pl3 summaries report roughly 98–100% training success under different architecture, reward, horizon and budget. Those saved training values are not independently reproduced held-out results and are excluded from the matched tables. Recovered legacy-run inventory.

Evidence-based status: camera access improves observed performance in the original matched seed, with initial positioning above continuous active control. Optimization repair improves static aggregate performance, while universal XM failure and numerical variability prevent a claim of reliable insertion. The first transfer pilot has also failed to demonstrate competence; pushing remains untrained.
